rows.question: Does the technical documentation of a high-risk AI system require to provide specifications regarding the required hardware?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 11, a provider must draw up technical documentation containing the information set out in Annex IV, which expressly requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV point 1(e)) and, as part of the system's development description, the computational resources used to develop, train, test and validate it (Annex IV point 2(c)).

rows.question: I have a medical device that has an AI system as a safety component. The medical device is classified "medium-risk" and undergoes a 3rd party conformity assessment. Is the AI system "medium risk" too? If yes, why? If not, why not?
rows.answer: No. The AI system is high-risk under the AI Act; there is no "medium-risk" classification in Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, and the MDR risk class of the host device does not transfer to the AI system. Classification under Article 6(1) turns on two cumulative conditions, both of which the operator's facts satisfy: (a) the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices is listed at Annex I, point 11 (and the IVDR at point 12), both in Section A; and (b) that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service under that legislation. The operator's device's "medium-risk" MDR class is legally relevant only because it is what triggers the notified-body route; once a third-party assessment is required, condition (b) is met and the classification is binary, high-risk, with no gradation tracking Class IIa versus Class III. Article 6(1) applies irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of that product. Two further points follow. First, the Article 6(3) derogation (narrow procedural task, improving a previously completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing human assessment, or a preparatory task, and never available where the system profiles natural persons) is a derogation from Article 6(2) only; it is unavailable to an Annex I safety component, so there is no route to escape high-risk status here. Second, being high-risk does not mean a separate assessment: under Article 43(3) the provider follows the MDR conformity assessment procedure, the Chapter III Section 2 requirements (Articles 8 to 15, including the Article 9 risk-management system, Article 10 data governance, and Article 13 transparency and instructions for use) apply and form part of that assessment, and points 4.3, 4.4, 4.5 and the fifth paragraph of point 4.6 of Annex VII also apply, giving the MDR notified body access to training, validation and testing datasets, the power to require further evidence or tests or run its own, reasoned access to the training and trained models as a last resort, and the obligation to re-assess changes. Article 8(2) lets you integrate the AI Act testing, reporting, information and documentation into the operator's existing MDR documentation and procedures. Where the MDR would let the manufacturer opt out of third-party assessment because all harmonised standards were applied, that option may be used only if harmonised standards or common specifications covering all Section 2 requirements have also been applied, and taking that option would, by removing condition (b), remove the Article 6(1) basis for high-risk status. A substantial modification requires a new conformity assessment under Article 43(4), though pre-determined changes documented in the technical documentation for a continuously learning system do not count as substantial.

Condition (a): AI system is safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation (medical devices under Regulation (EU) 2017/745)
Condition (b): that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment
Both conditions cumulative under Article 6(1), irrespective of the device's own sectoral risk classification

rows.question: We want to deploy an AI system that performs biometric verification solely to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be. Is this system prohibited? Is it high-risk?
rows.answer: No, this system is not prohibited, and no, it is not high-risk on the biometrics route. One-to-one biometric verification whose sole purpose is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be is expressly carved out of Annex III, point 1(a), which lists remote biometric identification systems as a high-risk use case but states that this "shall not include AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification the sole purpose of which is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be". Because the system is therefore not an AI system referred to in Annex III at all, Article 6(2) is not triggered and the Article 6(3) derogation, with its four alternative conditions (narrow procedural task; improvement of a previously completed human activity; detection of decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing an uncertain human assessment absent proper human review; preparatory task to an Annex III assessment) and its counter-rule that an Annex III system performing profiling of natural persons is always high-risk, never needs to be tested. Nor is the practice caught by any limb of Article 5(1). Verification against a claimed identity is not a biometric categorisation system categorising individuals to deduce or infer race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation under Article 5(1)(g), and it is not "real-time" remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes under Article 5(1)(h), a prohibition that in any event admits the exhaustive exceptions in points (h)(i) targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation, and search for missing persons; (h)(ii) prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety, or a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack; and (h)(iii) localisation or identification of a suspect for the purpose of a criminal investigation, prosecution or execution of a criminal penalty for an Annex II offence punishable in the Member State concerned by at least four years' custody, that point being without prejudice to Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 for processing of biometric data for non-law-enforcement purposes. The remaining prohibitions, Article 5(1)(a) subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques causing significant harm, (b) exploitation of vulnerabilities of age, disability or a specific social or economic situation, (c) social scoring leading to detrimental treatment in unrelated contexts or disproportionate to the social behaviour, (d) criminal-offence risk assessment based solely on profiling or personality traits, (e), and (f), are equally unengaged by a pure identity check. Three qualifications bound that conclusion. First, the carve-out is purpose-specific: it holds only while verification is the sole purpose, so if the same system also performs biometric categorisation by sensitive or protected attributes (Annex III, point 1(b)) or emotion recognition (Annex III, point 1(c)), or is repurposed for one-to-many identification, the exclusion falls away and Annex III, point 1 applies. Second, Annex III, point 1 applies only "in so far as [biometrics] use is permitted under relevant Union or national law", and the exclusion from high-risk classification does not authorise processing that Union or national data protection law forbids. Third, the Annex III route is not the only one: under Article 6(1) the system would still be high-risk if it is a product, or the safety component of a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation, which is not the case for ordinary access-control or identity-proofing deployments. On transparency, Article 50(3) does not bite, because it addresses deployers of emotion recognition and biometric categorisation systems only, and verification is neither. If the system is intended to interact directly with natural persons, the provider must under Article 50(1) design it so that the persons concerned are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person in the circumstances and context of use, and that duty does not apply to systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for third parties' rights and freedoms, unless the system is available to the public to report a criminal offence; any such information must be given clearly and distinguishably at the latest at the time of first interaction and must meet applicable accessibility requirements (Article 50(5)), without prejudice to Chapter III requirements or other Union or national transparency obligations (Article 50(6)).

rows.question: Which article of the EU AI Act governs human oversight measures?
rows.answer: Human oversight of high-risk AI systems is governed by Article 14 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. Article 14(1) requires high-risk AI systems to be designed and developed, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, so that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use. Under Article 14(2), that oversight must aim to prevent or minimise risks to health, safety or fundamental rights arising from use in accordance with the intended purpose or under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse, in particular where such risks persist despite the other requirements of that Section. Article 14(3) requires the measures to be commensurate with the risks, level of autonomy and context of use, and to be ensured through either or both of (a) measures identified and built into the system by the provider, when technically feasible, before it is placed on the market or put into service, and (b) measures identified by the provider before placing on the market or putting into service that are appropriate for implementation by the deployer. Article 14(4) requires the system to be supplied to the deployer so that the natural persons assigned oversight are enabled, as appropriate and proportionate, to: (a) properly understand the system's relevant capacities and limitations and duly monitor its operation, including detecting and addressing anomalies, dysfunctions and unexpected performance; (b) remain aware of the possible tendency to rely or over-rely automatically on the output (automation bias), in particular where the system provides information or recommendations for decisions taken by natural persons; (c) correctly interpret the system's output, taking into account the available interpretation tools and methods; (d) decide, in any particular situation, not to use the system or to otherwise disregard, override or reverse its output; and (e) intervene in the system's operation or interrupt it through a 'stop' button or similar procedure allowing the system to halt in a safe state. Article 14(5) adds, for the remote biometric identification systems referred to in point 1(a) of Annex III, that no action or decision may be taken by the deployer on the basis of an identification resulting from the system unless that identification has been separately verified and confirmed by at least two natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority; that two-person verification requirement does not apply to high-risk AI systems used for law enforcement, migration, border control or asylum purposes where Union or national law considers its application disproportionate.

Overseers enabled to understand, monitor, interpret, override, and halt the system

rows.question: Under what conditions should providers of general-purpose AI models be subject to exceptions regarding transparency-related requirements, if any? And what do those exceptions not cover?
rows.answer: The exceptions to the GPAI transparency-related obligations are set out in Article 53(2). The Article 53(1)(a) duty to draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model (Annex XI) and the Article 53(1)(b) duty to provide information and documentation to downstream providers (Annex XII) do not apply to providers that release the model under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution, where the model parameters, including the weights, and information on the model architecture and usage, are made publicly available. The exception does not cover the remaining Article 53(1) obligations: the policy to comply with Union copyright law (Article 53(1)(c)) and the publicly available, sufficiently detailed summary of the training content (Article 53(1)(d)) apply regardless of the licence. The exception also does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk (Article 53(2), second subparagraph), which remain subject to the full Article 53 obligations together with the Article 55 systemic-risk duties.

rows.question: What are the administrative fines for non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices?
rows.answer: Non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices in Article 5 is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Article 99(3)). This is the highest of the Regulation's three ceilings and applies to breach of any of the practices prohibited by Article 5(1), points (a) to (h), subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques causing significant harm; exploitation of vulnerabilities due to age, disability or a specific social or economic situation; social scoring producing detrimental treatment in unrelated contexts or disproportionate to the social behaviour; criminal-risk assessment based solely on profiling or personality traits; untargeted scraping of facial images to build facial-recognition databases; emotion inference in the workplace and in education institutions; biometric categorisation deducing sensitive attributes; and 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes. The Article 99(3) ceiling is distinct from, and higher than, the EUR 15 000 000 / 3 % ceiling that applies to the closed list of operator and notified-body obligations expressly "other than those laid down in Article 5" (Article 99(4)), and the EUR 7 500 000 / 1 % ceiling for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to notified bodies or national competent authorities (Article 99(5)). Two qualifications govern the amount actually imposed. Where the offender is an SME, including a start-up, the Article 99(3) ceiling is the lower of the percentage and the fixed amount rather than the higher (Article 99(6)). And each fine must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive, taking into account the interests of SMEs and start-ups and their economic viability (Article 99(1)), with the decision whether to fine and the amount determined in each individual case on the basis of all relevant circumstances listed in Article 99(7): the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement and its consequences, having regard to the purpose of the AI system and, where appropriate, the number of affected persons and the level of damage; whether other market surveillance authorities have already applied fines to the same operator for the same infringement; whether other authorities have already applied fines to the same operator for infringements of other Union or national law, where those result from the same activity or omission; the size, annual turnover and market share of the operator; any other aggravating or mitigating factor, such as financial benefits gained or losses avoided; the degree of cooperation with the national competent authorities to remedy the infringement and mitigate its adverse effects; the degree of responsibility of the operator, taking into account the technical and organisational measures it implemented; the manner in which the infringement became known to the authorities, in particular whether the operator notified it and to what extent; the intentional or negligent character of the infringement; and any action taken by the operator to mitigate the harm suffered by the affected persons. The fines themselves are laid down by the Member States, which must lay down the rules on penalties and other enforcement measures and take all measures necessary to ensure they are properly and effectively implemented, and notify the Commission of those rules (Article 99(1) and (2)); depending on the legal system of the Member State, the rules on administrative fines may be applied by national courts or other bodies as applicable in that Member State (Article 99(9)), and the exercise of these powers is subject to appropriate procedural safeguards in accordance with Union and national law, including effective judicial remedies and due process (Article 99(10)).

rows.question: What is a deep fake according to the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: ‘deep fake’ means AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful;

rows.question: What are all the risk categories in the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: The EU AI Act sets four risk tiers plus a separate regime for general-purpose AI models: unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5; and high-risk systems are classified under Article 6 (an Annex I product safety component, or an Annex III use case) and carry the Chapter III Section 2 obligations. Limited-risk systems carry the Article 50 transparency duties, minimal-risk systems avoid Chapter III high-risk requirements but retain Article 4 AI literacy duties, with voluntary codes under Article 95, and general-purpose AI models are governed separately under Articles 51 to 56, with added obligations under Article 55 for models classified as having systemic risk under Article 51.

rows.question: Can an operator that is not a provider according to the EU AI Act, for example a deployer, take actions on a given high-risk AI system such that it can be effectively seen as a provider by the authorities? If yes, what kind of action would result in such an outcome?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 25(1), a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is deemed to be the provider of a high-risk AI system, and takes on the provider obligations in Article 16, in any of three cases. First, if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market (Article 25(1)(a)). Second, if it makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk (Article 25(1)(b)). Third, if it modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk (Article 25(1)(c)). In each of these three cases the operator assumes the provider obligations in Article 16, and the initial provider is no longer considered the provider of that specific system under Article 25(2).

rows.question: According to Article 1, what is the objective of the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: Article 1 states the Regulation's purpose as improving the functioning of the internal market and promoting the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI, while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection, against the harmful effects of AI systems in the Union, and supporting innovation (Article 1(1)). To that end, the Regulation lays down harmonised rules for the placing on the market, the putting into service and the use of AI systems in the Union; prohibitions of certain AI practices; specific requirements for high-risk AI systems and obligations for operators of such systems; harmonised transparency rules for certain AI systems; harmonised rules for the placing on the market of general-purpose AI models; rules on market monitoring, market surveillance, governance and enforcement; and measures to support innovation, with a particular focus on SMEs, including start-ups (Article 1(2)).

rows.question: Is an AI system used to structure or deduplicate information for a use case listed in Annex III considered high-risk?
rows.answer: No. Structuring or deduplicating information is a narrow procedural task, so the system falls under the Article 6(3) first subparagraph point (a) derogation and is not high-risk, provided it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and does not materially influence the outcome of decision making; the other limbs are (b) improving the result of a previously completed human activity, (c) detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, and (d) performing a preparatory task, and the derogation never applies where the system profiles natural persons. Under Article 6(4) a provider relying on the derogation must document the assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, and register it under Article 49(2).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what jurisdiction does the Court of Justice of the European Union have over Commission decisions fixing fines on providers of general-purpose AI models, and what can the Court do with the fine?
rows.answer: The Court of Justice of the European Union has unlimited jurisdiction to review decisions of the Commission fixing a fine on providers of general-purpose AI models, and in exercising it the Court may cancel, reduce or increase the fine imposed (Article 101(5)). Unlimited jurisdiction goes beyond ordinary annulment review of legality: the Court may substitute its own assessment of the amount for the Commission's, which is why the power expressly extends upwards as well as downwards. The decisions subject to that review are those adopted under Article 101(1), by which the Commission may fine a provider of a general-purpose AI model up to 3 % of its annual total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher, where it finds the provider intentionally or negligently: (a) infringed the relevant provisions of the Regulation; (b) failed to comply with a request for a document or for information pursuant to Article 91, or supplied incorrect, incomplete or misleading information; (c) failed to comply with a measure requested under Article 93; or (d) failed to make available to the Commission access to the general-purpose AI model, or the general-purpose AI model with systemic risk, with a view to an evaluation pursuant to Article 92. In fixing the amount, regard must be had to the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement, with due account of proportionality and appropriateness, and to commitments made under Article 93(3) or in codes of practice under Article 56, the same criteria the Court reviews and may reapply when it sets the fine itself. The Commission must first communicate its preliminary findings and give the provider an opportunity to be heard (Article 101(2)), and the fine must in any event be effective, proportionate and dissuasive (Article 101(3)).

rows.question: When registering a high-risk AI system in the EU database under the EU AI Act, what specific information must the provider submit? List the required items.
rows.answer: A provider placing a high-risk Annex III system on the market or putting it into service must, beforehand, register both itself and the system in the EU database (Article 49(1)), and must enter the data listed in Section A of Annex VIII (Article 71(2)). The exhaustive list of Section A items is: (1) the name, address and contact details of the provider; (2) where submission is carried out by another person on the provider's behalf, that person's name, address and contact details; (3) the name, address and contact details of the authorised representative, where applicable; (4) the AI system trade name and any additional unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability of the system; (5) a description of the intended purpose of the AI system and of the components and functions supported through it; (6) a basic and concise description of the information used by the system (data, inputs) and its operating logic; (7) the status of the AI system (on the market, or in service; no longer placed on the market/in service, recalled); (8) the type, number and expiry date of the certificate issued by the notified body and the name or identification number of that notified body, where applicable; (9) a scanned copy of the certificate referred to in point 8, where applicable; (10) any Member States in which the AI system has been placed on the market, put into service or made available in the Union; (11) a copy of the EU declaration of conformity; (12) electronic instructions for use; and (13) a URL for additional information, which is optional. Point 12 is expressly not to be provided for high-risk systems in the areas of law enforcement or migration, asylum and border control management referred to in Annex III, points 1, 6 and 7 (Annex VIII, point 12). Registration also entails the names and contact details of the natural persons responsible for registering the system who have legal authority to represent the provider (Article 71(5)). Three qualifications shape that duty. First, systems falling under point 2 of Annex III (critical infrastructure) are excluded from Article 49(1) and are registered at national level instead (Article 49(5)). Second, for high-risk systems referred to in points 1, 6 and 7 of Annex III, registration is made in a secure non-public section of the database and includes only Section A, points 1 to 10, with the exception of points 6, 8 and 9, access being limited to the Commission and the national authorities referred to in Article 74(8) (Article 49(4)(a)). Third, a provider that has concluded under Article 6(3) that its Annex III system is not high-risk must still register itself and that system, supplying the Section B information instead (Article 49(2), Article 6(4), Article 71(2)); where such a system falls in the law-enforcement, migration, asylum or border-control areas, that registration is confined to Section B, points 1 to 5 and points 8 and 9 (Article 49(4)(b)). Section C is populated separately by deployers that are public authorities, Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies, or persons acting on their behalf, which must register themselves, select the system and register its use (Article 49(3), Article 71(3)).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, when a high-risk AI system is found to conform with the requirements, what information must the Union technical documentation assessment certificate contain?
rows.answer: Under Annex VII point 4.6, where the notified body finds the high-risk AI system conforms with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, it issues a Union technical documentation assessment certificate. Per Annex VII point 4.6, that certificate must indicate the name and address of the provider, the conclusions of the examination, the conditions (if any) for its validity, and the data necessary for the identification of the AI system. Under Article 44(1) the certificate must be drawn up in a language which can be easily understood by the relevant authorities in the Member State in which the notified body is established, and under Article 44(2) it is valid for the period it indicates, which may not exceed five years for AI systems covered by Annex I and four years for AI systems covered by Annex III.

rows.question: Under Article 10(5) of the EU AI Act, when may a provider of a high-risk AI system process special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction, and what key safeguards/conditions must be met?
rows.answer: Under Article 10(5), a provider of a high-risk AI system may exceptionally process special categories of personal data only to the extent strictly necessary to ensure bias detection and correction, subject to appropriate safeguards. These conditions apply in addition to, and not instead of, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680. Article 10(5) requires all of the following: the bias work cannot be done with other data, including synthetic or anonymised data (a); technical limits on re-use plus state-of-the-art security and pseudonymisation (b); strict controls and documentation of access so that only authorised persons under appropriate confidentiality obligations can reach the data (c); the data are not transmitted, transferred or otherwise accessed by other parties (d); deletion once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends, whichever is first (e); and records of processing documenting why it was strictly necessary (f).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must a provider of a high-risk AI system supply to the deployer in the instructions for use? List the required categories of information.
rows.answer: A provider of a high‑risk AI system must accompany it with instructions for use in an appropriate digital or other format, containing concise, complete, correct and clear information that is relevant, accessible and comprehensible to deployers (Article 13(1) and (2)). Article 13(3) fixes the minimum content, which falls into six categories. First, the identity and contact details of the provider and, where applicable, of its authorised representative (Article 13(3)(a)). Second, the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance of the system (Article 13(3)(b)), comprising seven sub‑points: its intended purpose; the level of accuracy, including its metrics, robustness and cybersecurity referred to in Article 15 against which the system has been tested and validated and which can be expected, together with any known or foreseeable circumstances that may affect that expected level; any known or foreseeable circumstance, related to use in accordance with the intended purpose or under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse, which may lead to risks to health and safety or fundamental rights referred to in Article 9(2); where applicable, the technical capabilities and characteristics of the system to provide information relevant to explaining its output; when appropriate, its performance regarding specific persons or groups of persons on which the system is intended to be used; when appropriate, specifications for the input data or other relevant information on the training, validation and testing data sets used, having regard to the intended purpose; and, where applicable, information enabling deployers to interpret the output and use it appropriately. Third, the changes to the system and its performance pre‑determined by the provider at the moment of the initial conformity assessment, if any (Article 13(3)(c)). Fourth, the human oversight measures referred to in Article 14, including the technical measures put in place to facilitate deployers' interpretation of the system's outputs (Article 13(3)(d)). Fifth, the computational and hardware resources needed, the expected lifetime of the system, and any necessary maintenance and care measures, including their frequency, to ensure proper functioning, including as regards software updates (Article 13(3)(e)). Sixth, where relevant, a description of the mechanisms included within the system that allow deployers to properly collect, store and interpret the logs in accordance with Article 12 (Article 13(3)(f)). These instructions are also the vehicle through which the provider discharges the information element of its risk‑management duty under Article 9(5)(c), and the declared accuracy metrics required by Article 15 must appear there; supplying them is part of ensuring compliance with the Section 2 requirements under Articles 8 and 16(1)(a). And, where the provider also relies on them to eliminate or reduce residual risk, the instructions must be drafted with due regard to the technical knowledge, experience, education and training to be expected of the deployer and the presumable context of use, with training provided to deployers where appropriate.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) Article 95, who may draw up codes of conduct, and which bodies must encourage and facilitate their drawing up?
rows.answer: Codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, by organisations representing them, or by both, including with the involvement of any interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society organisations and academia; such codes may cover one or more AI systems, taking into account the similarity of the intended purpose of the relevant systems (Article 95(3)). The bodies under the duty to encourage and facilitate are the AI Office and the Member States. Under Article 95(1) they must encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct, including related governance mechanisms, intended to foster the voluntary application to AI systems other than high-risk AI systems of some or all of the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2, taking into account available technical solutions and industry best practices. Under Article 95(2) the AI Office and the Member States must also facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct concerning the voluntary application, including by deployers, of specific requirements to all AI systems, on the basis of clear objectives and key performance indicators to measure the achievement of those objectives, including elements such as applicable elements of Union ethical guidelines for trustworthy AI; assessing and minimising the impact of AI systems on environmental sustainability, including energy-efficient programming and efficient design, training and use; promoting AI literacy, in particular of persons dealing with the development, operation and use of AI; facilitating inclusive and diverse design of AI systems, including inclusive and diverse development teams and the promotion of stakeholders' participation; and assessing and preventing the negative impact of AI systems on vulnerable persons or groups, including as regards accessibility for persons with a disability, as well as on gender equality. When encouraging and facilitating the drawing up of codes of conduct, the AI Office and the Member States must take into account the specific interests and needs of SMEs, including start-ups (Article 95(4)).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what minimum elements must a provider's quality management system (QMS) for high-risk AI systems include? List the required elements.
rows.answer: A provider of a high-risk AI system must put in place a quality management system that ensures compliance with the Regulation and is documented in a systematic and orderly manner in the form of written policies, procedures and instructions, covering at least thirteen aspects (Article 17(1)): (a) a strategy for regulatory compliance, including compliance with conformity assessment procedures and procedures for managing modifications to the system; (b) techniques, procedures and systematic actions for the design, design control and design verification of the system; (c) techniques, procedures and systematic actions for development, quality control and quality assurance; (d) examination, test and validation procedures to be carried out before, during and after development, and the frequency with which they are to be carried out; (e) technical specifications, including standards, to be applied and, where harmonised standards are not applied in full or do not cover all relevant requirements, the means used to ensure compliance with the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements; (f) systems and procedures for data management, including data acquisition, collection, analysis, labelling, storage, filtration, mining, aggregation, retention and any other data operation performed before and for the purpose of placing on the market or putting into service; (g) the risk management system referred to in Article 9; (h) the setting-up, implementation and maintenance of a post-market monitoring system in accordance with Article 72; (i) procedures related to the reporting of a serious incident in accordance with Article 73; (j) the handling of communication with national competent authorities, other relevant authorities including those providing or supporting access to data, notified bodies, other operators, customers or other interested parties; (k) systems and procedures for record-keeping of all relevant documentation and information; (l) resource management, including security-of-supply related measures; and (m) an accountability framework setting out the responsibilities of management and other staff with regard to all of those aspects. Implementation of these aspects must be proportionate to the size of the provider's organisation, but providers must in any event respect the degree of rigour and level of protection required to ensure their high-risk AI systems comply with the Regulation (Article 17(2)). Providers already subject to quality management system obligations or an equivalent function under relevant sectoral Union law may incorporate the Article 17(1) aspects into that existing system (Article 17(3)). For providers that are financial institutions subject to internal governance, arrangements or process requirements under Union financial services law, the obligation to put a quality management system in place is deemed fulfilled by complying with those internal governance rules, with the exception of points (g), (h) and (i), the risk management system, post-market monitoring and serious-incident reporting, which remain mandatory; harmonised standards referred to in Article 40 are to be taken into account for that purpose (Article 17(4)).

Design, development, quality control and verification techniques/procedures
Examination, test and validation procedures and their frequency
Data management procedures across data lifecycle
Article 9 risk management system and Article 72 post-market monitoring system
Record-keeping and accountability framework for management/staff

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, in which specific situations may law enforcement use 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes (i.e., the exceptions to the prohibition)? List the permitted objectives.
rows.answer: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes is prohibited by Article 5(1)(h) save where, and only in so far as, such use is strictly necessary for one of three exhaustively listed objectives. Those objectives are: (i) the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation of human beings, as well as the search for missing persons; (ii) the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons, or of a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack; and (iii) the localisation or identification of a person suspected of having committed a criminal offence, for the purpose of conducting a criminal investigation or prosecution or executing a criminal penalty, for offences referred to in Annex II and punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or a detention order for a maximum period of at least four years (Article 5(1)(h)(i), (iii)). The Annex II list comprises terrorism, trafficking in human beings, sexual exploitation of children and child sexual abuse material, illicit trafficking in narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances, illicit trafficking in weapons, munitions or explosives, murder, grievous bodily injury, illicit trade in human organs or tissue, illicit trafficking in nuclear or radioactive materials, kidnapping, illegal restraint or hostage-taking, crimes within the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court, unlawful seizure of aircraft or ships, rape, environmental crime, organised or armed robbery, sabotage, and participation in a criminal organisation involved in one or more of those offences. Article 5(1)(h) is without prejudice to Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 as regards processing of biometric data for purposes other than law enforcement. These are objectives-based carve-outs, not a general permission: under Article 5(2) the system may be deployed only to confirm the identity of the specifically targeted individual, and the deploying authority must take into account the nature of the situation giving rise to the possible use, in particular the seriousness, probability and scale of the harm that would be caused if the system were not used, and the consequences of the use for the rights and freedoms of all persons concerned, in particular the seriousness, probability and scale of those consequences. The use must comply with necessary and proportionate safeguards and conditions laid down in the authorising national law, in particular as regards temporal, geographic and personal limitations, and is authorised only where the law-enforcement authority has completed a fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 and has registered the system in the EU database under Article 49, although in duly justified cases of urgency use may begin before registration provided registration is completed without undue delay. Article 5(3) further requires prior authorisation granted by a judicial authority or by an independent administrative authority whose decision is binding, issued upon reasoned request and in accordance with the detailed rules of national law; in a duly justified situation of urgency the use may be started without authorisation, but the authorisation must be requested without undue delay and at the latest within 24 hours, and where it is refused the use must be stopped with immediate effect and all data, results and output discarded and deleted. Under Article 5(4) each use must be notified to the relevant market surveillance authority and the national data protection authority, and Member States may, pursuant to Article 5(5), decide whether to provide at all for the possibility of authorising such use within the limits of Article 5(1)(h) and Articles 5(2) and (3), the Regulation permits but does not oblige them to do so. Non-compliance with these prohibitions attracts the highest penalty tier of up to EUR 35 million or 7 % of total worldwide annual turnover under Article 99(3).

Prevention of specific, substantial and imminent threat to life/physical safety, or genuine terrorist attack threat
Localisation/identification of a suspect for investigation, prosecution, or executing a penalty for an Annex II offence punishable by at least 4 years custodial sentence/detention order

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must providers of AI systems that generate or manipulate synthetic content do to enable identification of AI-generated/manipulated output, and what quality criteria must that solution meet?
rows.answer: Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text content must ensure that the outputs of the system are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(2)). The marking duty attaches to the provider at the design level, so it must be built into the system's outputs rather than left to the deployer, and it is without prejudice to the Chapter III requirements and to other transparency obligations in Union or national law (Article 50(6)). The technical solution used for that marking must meet four cumulative quality criteria: it must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable. Those criteria apply "as far as this is technically feasible", and feasibility is judged by reference to the specificities and limitations of the various types of content, the costs of implementation, and the generally acknowledged state of the art, as may be reflected in relevant technical standards (Article 50(2)). The obligation is subject to three carve-outs, also in Article 50(2): it does not apply to the extent that the AI systems perform an assistive function for standard editing; to the extent that they do not substantially alter the input data provided by the deployer or the semantics thereof; or where the systems are authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences. Where the marking under Article 50(2) also operates as information to natural persons, that information must be provided in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure and must conform to the applicable accessibility requirements (Article 50(5)). Compliance detail is to be further supported by codes of practice at Union level, which the AI Office encourages and facilitates for the detection and labelling of artificially generated or manipulated content; the Commission may approve such codes by implementing act under the procedure in Article 56(6), and, if it deems a code inadequate, may instead specify common rules for the implementation of those obligations by implementing act under Article 98(2) (Article 50(7)).

Exemptions: assistive editing, no substantial alteration of input data/semantics, or law-enforcement authorisation

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, which body has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models (Chapter V), and which entity is entrusted with implementing those tasks?
rows.answer: The European Commission holds exclusive powers to supervise and enforce the Chapter V obligations of providers of general-purpose AI models, and it entrusts the implementation of those tasks to the AI Office (Article 88(1)). Those exclusive powers are exercised taking into account the procedural guarantees under Article 94, and the entrustment to the AI Office operates without prejudice to the Commission's own powers of organisation and to the division of competences between the Member States and the Union under the Treaties (Article 88(1)). The exclusivity is therefore institutional rather than absolute in practice: national market surveillance authorities retain no supervisory competence over Chapter V itself, but, without prejudice to Article 75(3), they may request the Commission to exercise the powers laid down in that Section where doing so is necessary and proportionate to assist them in fulfilling their own tasks under the Regulation (Article 88(2)). This matters in particular where a general-purpose AI model is integrated into an AI system falling within those authorities' competence under Article 74. Correspondingly, providers of general-purpose AI models must cooperate as necessary with the Commission and the national competent authorities in the exercise of their respective competences and powers (Article 53(3)), and the Article 53(1)(a) technical documentation is to be provided, upon request, to the AI Office and the national competent authorities. Providers of models with systemic risk report serious incidents and possible corrective measures to the AI Office and, as appropriate, to national competent authorities (Article 55(1)(c)), and a provider that adheres to neither an approved code of practice nor a European harmonised standard must demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance for assessment by the Commission (Articles 53(4) and 55(2)). Enforcement of Chapter V itself, however, remains with the Commission acting through the AI Office (Article 88(1)).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what conditions must be met before data collected and processed for testing high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions can be transferred to a third country (outside the EU)?
rows.answer: Data collected and processed for the purpose of testing in real world conditions may be transferred to third countries only provided that appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law are implemented (Article 60(4)(e)). That is the whole of the transfer condition the Act imposes: it does not create a bespoke transfer regime but conditions any export on compliance with the safeguards that Union law, principally Union data protection law, already requires for the transfer in question, and those safeguards must be both appropriate to the transfer and applicable to it. This condition is cumulative, not free-standing: Article 60(4) permits a provider or prospective provider to conduct the testing at all only where all of its listed conditions are met, so the transfer is lawful only within a testing exercise that itself satisfies the remaining limbs, a real-world testing plan drawn up and submitted to the market surveillance authority of the Member State where the testing is to be conducted (point (a)); approval of the testing and the plan by that authority, with tacit approval after 30 days unless national law does not provide for tacit approval, in which case an authorisation remains required (point (b)); registration of the testing with a Union-wide unique single identification number and the information specified in Annex IX under Article 71(4), or, for Annex III points 1, 6 and 7 systems in law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control management, in the secure non-public section of the EU database under Article 49(4), point (d), and, for Annex III point 2 systems, in accordance with Article 49(5) (point (c)); establishment of the provider or prospective provider in the Union or appointment of a legal representative established in the Union (point (d)); and informed consent of the subjects of the testing in accordance with Article 61, save that in law enforcement, where seeking informed consent would prevent the system from being tested, the testing and its outcome must have no negative effect on the subjects and their personal data must be deleted after the test is performed (point (i)), alongside the further conditions in points (f), (g), (h), (j) and (k). Two related data duties continue to bind after any transfer: subjects may withdraw from the testing at any time by revoking their informed consent, without detriment and without justification, and may request the immediate and permanent deletion of their personal data, the withdrawal not affecting activities already carried out (Article 60(5)); and the testing remains without prejudice to any ethical review required by Union or national law (Article 60(3)). The Act specifies no adequacy-style mechanism, no derogation and no authority-specific clearance for the transfer itself beyond the safeguards requirement in Article 60(4)(e).

rows.question: What are the conditions to classify general-purpose AI (GPAI) model as "GPAI model with systemic risk"? Do all need to be met at the same time?
rows.answer: No, the conditions are alternatives, not cumulative. Article 51(1) provides that a general-purpose AI model is classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk if it meets any of the listed conditions, so satisfying one suffices. The two conditions are: (a) it has high impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks (Article 51(1)(a)); or (b) on the basis of a decision of the Commission, taken ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, it has capabilities or an impact equivalent to those in point (a), having regard to the criteria set out in Annex XIII (Article 51(1)(b)). Within limb (a), Article 51(2) adds a rebuttable presumption rather than a further cumulative requirement: a model is presumed to have high impact capabilities where the cumulative amount of computation used for its training, measured in floating-point operations, is greater than 10^25. "High-impact capabilities" are defined as capabilities that match or exceed the capabilities recorded in the most advanced general-purpose AI models (Article 3(64)), and "systemic risk" as a risk specific to those high-impact capabilities, having a significant impact on the Union market due to their reach, or due to actual or reasonably foreseeable negative effects on public health, safety, public security, fundamental rights, or society as a whole, that can be propagated at scale across the value chain (Article 3(65)). Article 51(3) empowers the Commission to amend, by delegated acts, the thresholds in paragraphs 1 and 2 and to supplement the benchmarks and indicators in light of evolving technological developments. Logically prior to either limb, the model must first qualify as a general-purpose AI model within the meaning of Article 3(63). Meeting either limb triggers the Article 55(1) obligations in addition to those in Articles 53 and 54, model evaluation in accordance with standardised protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, including documented adversarial testing; assessment and mitigation of possible systemic risks at Union level, including their sources; tracking, documenting and reporting serious incidents and possible corrective measures without undue delay to the AI Office and, as appropriate, to national competent authorities; and ensuring an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure, and it removes the free and open-source exemption, since the disapplication of Article 53(1), points (a) and (b), expressly does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk (Article 53(2)).

Condition (b): Commission decision (ex officio or following qualified alert from scientific panel) that capabilities/impact are equivalent, per Annex XIII criteria
No, not cumulative - either condition alone suffices

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, is an AI system that is a safety component of a medical device classified as MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) automatically a high-risk AI system? Explain your reasoning.
rows.answer: No. An AI system that is a safety component of a medical device is not automatically high-risk merely because the device falls under the MDR; Article 6(1) makes classification conditional on two cumulative conditions, and a Class I device that is non-sterile, non-measuring and not a reusable surgical instrument satisfies only the first. Article 6(1)(a) is met: Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices is listed in Annex I, point 11, and the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by that Union harmonisation legislation. Article 6(1)(b), however, additionally requires that the product whose safety component the AI system is, or the AI system itself as a product, be required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service pursuant to that Annex I legislation. Class I devices in the plain category described are the one MDR class for which the manufacturer declares conformity without notified body involvement; notified body participation is triggered only by the sterile, measuring-function and reusable-surgical-instrument carve-outs, each of which is excluded by the facts. With no third-party conformity assessment required, the second cumulative condition fails and the Annex I route in Article 6(1) does not classify the system as high-risk, irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the device. That conclusion is confined to the Annex I product route. The system may still be high-risk under Article 6(2) if it is an AI system referred to in relevantly here, the area of access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits, which covers evaluation of eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services including healthcare services (point 5(a)), creditworthiness evaluation or credit scoring other than for financial-fraud detection (point 5(b)), risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in life and health insurance (point 5(c)), and evaluation and classification of emergency calls or the dispatching and prioritisation of emergency first response services, including emergency healthcare patient triage systems (point 5(d)); the other Annex III areas are biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and workers' management and access to self-employment, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control management, and administration of justice and democratic processes. If the system falls within a listed use case, the Article 6(3) derogation can still remove it from high-risk status where it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision-making, and it performs a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns or deviations from prior patterns without being meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment absent proper human review, or performs a preparatory task to a relevant assessment, but it is always high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons. A provider relying on that derogation must document its assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service, is subject to the registration obligation in Article 49(2), and must supply the documentation to national competent authorities on request (Article 6(4)). A caveat on classification inputs rather than on the rule: the MDR class stated in the question is assumed correct, and if the AI element causes the device to be reclassified above that plain Class I category, notified body involvement would be required and Article 6(1)(b) would then be satisfied.
criteria_text: No
Article 6(1)(a) and (b) are cumulative conditions
MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) devices undergo manufacturer self-assessment, not third-party conformity assessment
Condition (b) fails, so Article 6(1) does not apply
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states 'No' as its first word and maintains that position throughout, aligning with the required verdict.
The answer clearly states that Article 6(1) requires two 'cumulative conditions' and explains that both must be met, conveying the substance that the conditions are not standalone.

The answer explains that Class I devices in the specified category undergo manufacturer self-assessment without notified body involvement, directly stating the absence of third-party conformity assessment.
The answer concludes that because third-party assessment is not required, the second condition fails and thus Article 6(1) does not apply, which matches the substance of the criterion.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, can an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in a lift qualify as a high-risk AI system, and under what conditions?
rows.answer: Yes. An AI system intended to be used as a safety component in a lift can qualify as a high-risk AI system, but only under the Annex I product route in Article 6(1), and only where both of its cumulative conditions are met. First, under Article 6(1)(a), the AI system must be intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or be itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I. That condition is satisfied for lifts, because Annex I, point 4, lists Directive 2014/33/EU on the harmonisation of the laws of the Member States relating to lifts and safety components for lifts. Second, under Article 6(1)(b), the product whose safety component the AI system is, or the AI system itself as a product, must be required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service pursuant to that Annex I legislation. If the applicable procedure under Directive 2014/33/EU for the lift or for the safety component in question does not require third-party involvement, condition (b) fails and Article 6(1) does not classify the system as high-risk. Article 6(1) applies irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the lift or of the safety component, so a standalone AI safety component is caught on the same terms as one embedded in the lift. Because the classification arises under Article 6(1) and not under Article 6(2), the derogation in Article 6(3) is unavailable: it applies only to AI systems referred to in Annex III, and its conditions, a narrow procedural task, improving the result of a previously completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns or deviations from prior patterns without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment absent proper human review, or performing a preparatory task to an Annex III assessment, with profiling of natural persons always remaining high-risk, cannot be invoked for a lift safety component. Nor does the provider self-assessment documentation and Article 49(2) registration mechanism in Article 6(4), which is likewise confined to Annex III systems. As to the consequences for conformity assessment, Article 43(3) governs: for high-risk AI systems covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of which includes Directive 2014/33/EU, the provider follows the relevant conformity assessment procedure required under that legal act, and the requirements of Section 2 of Chapter III apply to the system and form part of that assessment, with points 4.3, 4.4, 4.5 and the fifth paragraph of point 4.6 of Annex VII also applying. Notified bodies notified under Directive 2014/33/EU are entitled to control conformity with the Section 2 requirements, provided their compliance with the requirements in Article 31(4), (5), (10) and (11) has been assessed in the notification procedure under that Directive. Where that Directive enables the product manufacturer to opt out of third-party conformity assessment on the basis that it has applied all harmonised standards covering the relevant requirements, the manufacturer may use that option only if it has also applied harmonised standards or, where applicable, common specifications under Article 41 covering all the Section 2 requirements. Under Article 43(4), a system already assessed must undergo a new conformity assessment in the event of a substantial modification, regardless of whether the modified system is further distributed or continues to be used by the current deployer; for systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or put into service, changes pre-determined by the provider at the initial assessment and recorded in the technical documentation under point 2(f) of Annex IV do not constitute a substantial modification. The internal-control route in Annex VI under Article 43(1) and (2) is reserved for Annex III systems and is not the applicable path here.
criteria_text: Yes
Condition: AI system intended as safety component of a product covered by Annex I Union harmonisation legislation
Condition: that product (or the AI system itself as a product) required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation
Both conditions cumulative

The answer states the AI system must be intended as a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation and cites Directive 2014/33/EU on lifts as falling under Annex I, thus conveying the substance of the condition.

The answer clearly explains that the product (or AI system as product) must be subject to third-party conformity assessment under the relevant Annex I legislation, and notes that if no third-party assessment is required, the condition fails.
The answer repeatedly emphasizes that both conditions under Article 6(1) are cumulative and must be jointly satisfied, using phrases like 'only where both of its cumulative conditions are met.'

rows.question: A provider becomes aware of a risk (within the meaning of Article 79(1)) for their high-risk AI system. Does the provider need to take immediate corrective action OR immediately investigate the causes OR both? For example, perhaps it's the market surveillance authority that must investigate the cause, and the provider can help later.
rows.answer: The two duties run in parallel and neither is deferred to the market surveillance authority. Under Article 20(1), a provider that considers or has reason to consider that a high-risk AI system it has placed on the market or put into service is not in conformity must immediately take the necessary corrective actions, bringing the system into conformity, withdrawing it, disabling it, or recalling it, as appropriate, and must inform the distributors and, where applicable, the deployers, the authorised representative and the importers. Under Article 20(2), where that system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) and the provider becomes aware of that risk, it must immediately investigate the causes, in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable, and inform the market surveillance authorities competent for the system concerned and, where applicable, the notified body that issued the Article 44 certificate, in particular of the nature of the non-compliance and of any relevant corrective action taken. The phrase "any relevant corrective action taken" presupposes that the Article 20(1) corrective action is already under way when the notification is made; the investigation duty is additional to it, not a substitute. The operator's alternative reading is wrong on the allocation of roles. The authority's evaluation under Article 79(2) is triggered by its own sufficient reason to consider that a system presents a risk, is directed at the system's compliance with all requirements and obligations of the Regulation, and results in the authority requiring the operator to take corrective action within a prescribed period, in any event within the shorter of 15 working days or the period set by the relevant Union harmonisation legislation. That public-law evaluation does not replace the provider's own causal investigation; Article 79(2) expressly requires the relevant operators to cooperate as necessary with the market surveillance authority and with the Article 77(1) bodies, and Article 79(4) requires the operator to ensure that all appropriate corrective action is taken in respect of all the AI systems concerned that it has made available on the Union market. Article 74(12) and (13) likewise assume the provider supplies documentation, data sets and, on reasoned request, once data- and documentation-based verification is exhausted, source code to support the authority's work; they do not transfer the investigation to the authority. Failure to take adequate corrective action within the Article 79(2) period exposes the provider to provisional measures under Article 79(5). Where the risk materialises as a serious incident, these duties are cumulative with Article 73: reporting to the market surveillance authority of the Member State where the incident occurred, immediately upon establishing a causal link or its reasonable likelihood and in any event within 15 days of awareness, reduced to two days for a widespread infringement or an Article 3(49)(b) incident and 10 days in the event of death, followed by the Article 73(6) duty to perform the necessary investigations without delay, including a risk assessment and corrective action, while not altering the system in a way that may affect any subsequent evaluation of the causes before informing the competent authorities.
criteria_text: Both
Immediate corrective action required under Article 20(1) where system is non-compliant
Immediate investigation of causes is the provider's own duty under Article 20(2)
Investigation done in collaboration with reporting deployer where applicable, not deferred to market surveillance authority
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that both duties—corrective action and investigation—run in parallel, satisfying the 'Both' criterion.

The answer cites Article 20(1) and describes the provider's duty to immediately take corrective action upon awareness of non-compliance, including bringing the system into conformity, withdrawing, disabling, or recalling it.
The answer clearly assigns the duty to immediately investigate the causes to the provider under Article 20(2), distinguishing it from the market surveillance authority's role.

The answer specifies that the investigation must be done in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable, and emphasizes that this duty lies with the provider, not the market surveillance authority.

rows.question: My local small language model says that, as a distributor of high-risk AI systems, I must be careful that transport conditions do not jeopardize compliance. But AI is just software, isn't it? So I am pretty sure my model hallucinated. What do you say?
rows.answer: The operator's model did not hallucinate. Article 24(3) says exactly that: distributors shall ensure that, while a high-risk AI system is under their responsibility, storage or transport conditions, where applicable, do not jeopardise the compliance of the system with the requirements set out in Section 2. The premise that "AI is just software" is what fails. A high-risk AI system is frequently placed on the market as, or embedded in, a physical item, a safety component of machinery, a medical device, a biometric terminal, an industrial controller, or delivered on physical media together with its CE marking, the copy of the EU declaration of conformity under Article 47 and the instructions for use that Article 24(1) requires the operator to verify before making it available. Physical handling can therefore degrade conformity: damaged or miscalibrated hardware, firmware altered or corrupted in transit, temperature or humidity exposure outside the provider's stated conditions, or loss of the accompanying documentation and instructions for use. The clause is deliberately qualified by "where applicable", so it simply does not bite for a system distributed purely as a download with no physical carrier, but that qualifier is a condition on the duty, not a denial that the duty exists. The obligation also has consequences the operator should plan for. If, on the basis of the information in the operator's possession, you consider or have reason to consider that the system is not in conformity with the Section 2 requirements, including because storage or transport has compromised it, the operator must not make it available on the market until it has been brought into conformity, and if it presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) the operator must inform the provider or the importer, as applicable (Article 24(2)). If the system has already been made available, the operator must take the corrective actions necessary to bring it into conformity, withdraw it or recall it, or ensure that the provider, the importer or any relevant operator takes those actions; and where it presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), immediately inform the provider or importer and the competent authorities, giving details of the non-compliance and of any corrective actions taken (Article 24(4)). On a reasoned request the operator must give the competent authority all information and documentation on the operator's actions under paragraphs 1 to 4 needed to demonstrate conformity (Article 24(5)), and cooperate with those authorities in any action they take on systems you made available, in particular to reduce or mitigate the risk (Article 24(6)).
criteria_text: No, not hallucinated
Article 24(3) applies
Duty applies only 'where applicable' (e.g., embedded/supplied hardware or physical media)

The answer directly cites and applies Article 24(3), confirming its relevance to the distributor's obligation.
The answer explains that the duty applies only 'where applicable', distinguishing cases involving physical media or hardware from pure software downloads.

rows.question: Does the AI Act prohibit or classifies as high-risk the use of AI in drones? Can I use AI in a drone to find who's around in town? And what if it's just a toy drone? And what about toy drones used for other applications?
rows.answer: The system described is not among the practices prohibited under Article 5 (social scoring, untargeted facial-image scraping, manipulative or exploitative techniques, and the other exhaustively-listed bans). Whether it is high-risk turns on Article 6: it is high-risk only if it is a safety component of a product regulated under Annex I (for example a medical device under the MDR or IVDR) or falls within one of the Annex III use cases. Otherwise it is limited- or minimal-risk, subject mainly to the Article 50 transparency duties where it interacts directly with people.
criteria_text: No blanket prohibition/high-risk classification for drones as such — turns on AI system's intended use under Article 6
Drone AI identifying people in public = remote biometric identification, high-risk under Annex III(1)(a), not the 1:1 verification exclusion
Toy status irrelevant — classification depends on intended use, not the device
Toy drone used for other application is high-risk only if that use matches Annex III (or Article 6(1) safety-component/conformity-assessment criteria)
criterion_remarks: The answer correctly states that drones are not automatically prohibited or high-risk, and that classification depends on intended use under Article 6.

The answer does not address that using AI in a drone to identify people in public constitutes remote biometric identification, which is high-risk under Annex III(1)(a); it omits this specific application and its consequences.
The answer fails to state that toy status is irrelevant for risk classification; it does not mention device categorization like 'toy drone' at all.
The answer does not specifically address toy drones used for other applications, nor does it assess such uses against Annex III or Article 6(1) criteria.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and clearly structured without self-reference or informality.

rows.question: We deployed a high-risk AI system in our company. We have a use in mind that is outside the intended use and our legal team say such a use is definitely no risk (no Annex I nor III apply). Can we just go ahead with the new use and do we need to keep logs for it?
rows.answer: No, you cannot simply proceed on the operator's legal team's classification view, and yes, the operator must keep the logs. The system you deployed was placed on the market as a high-risk AI system with a defined intended purpose, and Article 26(1) obliges you as deployer to take appropriate technical and organisational measures to use it in accordance with the instructions for use accompanying it. Those instructions state the intended purpose (Article 13(3)(b)(i)) and must also flag any known or foreseeable circumstance arising under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse that may lead to risks to health, safety or fundamental rights (Article 13(3)(b)(iii)). A use the provider did not contemplate falls outside the conformity assessment, the risk management system and the accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity envelope against which the system was validated, so deploying it there breaches Article 26(1) regardless of how the new use would classify if it were assessed from scratch. The operator's legal team's reasoning also addresses the wrong question. High-risk status attaches to the system as placed on the market, not to each downstream use, and a deployer has no power to reclassify it. The Annex I route under Article 6(1) turns on the system being a safety component of, or itself being, a product covered by the listed Union harmonisation legislation that must undergo third-party conformity assessment; the Annex III route under Article 6(2) turns on the system falling within a listed use case. The only declassification mechanism, the Article 6(3) derogation, is available solely for Annex III systems, requires that the system pose no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights including by not materially influencing decision-making outcomes, and requires one of four conditions, a narrow procedural task, improving the result of a previously completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns or deviations from prior patterns without being meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review, or a preparatory task to a relevant Annex III assessment, and never applies where the system performs profiling of natural persons. It is a provider self-assessment documented before the system is placed on the market, not a deployer judgement made after deployment. There is a further exposure: if adapting the system to the new use involves a substantial modification, or if you modify its intended purpose, Article 25(1) makes you a provider of a high-risk AI system and transfers the full provider obligations to you, with the initial provider owing you cooperation, information and technical access under Article 25(2). On logs, the duty is unchanged by the new use. Under Article 26(6) the operator must keep the logs automatically generated by the high-risk AI system, to the extent those logs are under the operator's control, for a period appropriate to the intended purpose and in any event at least six months, unless applicable Union or national law, in particular Union data protection law, provides otherwise; if the operator is a financial institution subject to internal governance, arrangements or process requirements under Union financial services law, you maintain the logs as part of the documentation kept under that legislation. The instructions for use should describe, where relevant, the mechanisms allowing you to collect, store and interpret those logs in accordance with Article 12 (Article 13(3)(f)). The correct path is to ask the provider to extend the intended purpose and re-assess, or to procure a system whose stated intended purpose covers the new use.
criteria_text: No, cannot proceed with the new use
Article 26(1) requires use in accordance with instructions for use; deviating from intended use is not excused merely because that use alone wouldn't trigger Annex III
Yes, logging duty under Article 26(6) still applies regardless of the particular use
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states that the deployer cannot proceed with the new use, aligning with the required 'No' verdict.

The answer explains that Article 26(1) requires use in accordance with instructions for use and that deviating from intended use violates this obligation, regardless of risk assessment of the new use.
The answer confirms that the logging duty under Article 26(6) applies regardless of the particular use, as long as the system remains high-risk and logs are under the deployer's control.
