rows.question: Is AI software that helps clinicians take medical decisions around best treatment potentially high-risk? According to what Article and/or Annex?
rows.answer: Yes. AI software that supports clinicians in deciding the best treatment is potentially high-risk, and in practice the decisive route is Article 6(1) rather than Annex III. Under Article 6(1), an AI system is high-risk, irrespective of whether it is placed on the market independently of the product, where both conditions are met: (a) it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I; and (b) that product, or the AI system itself as a product, is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that Annex I legislation. Clinical decision-support software of this kind is ordinarily software qualifying as a medical device under Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (Annex I, point 11), or, where it interprets in vitro diagnostic results, under Regulation (EU) 2017/746 (Annex I, point 12), and treatment-recommendation software is typically classified in a risk class requiring notified-body involvement. Where both limbs are satisfied, the system is high-risk by operation of Article 6(1), and the Article 6(3) derogation is unavailable, because that derogation applies only by derogation from Article 6(2), i.e. only to Annex III systems. The Annex III route (Article 6(2)) is a narrower fit. Treatment decision-support used by a clinician is not, as such, one of the listed uses: Annex III, point 5(a) captures AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate the eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, and to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim them; point 5(c) covers risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance; and point 5(d) covers evaluating and classifying emergency calls, dispatching or prioritising the dispatch of emergency first response services, including medical aid, as well as emergency healthcare patient triage systems. So an emergency triage or dispatch-prioritisation tool falls in Annex III, point 5(d), and an entitlement-to-care tool used by or for a public authority falls in point 5(a), whereas a bedside "best treatment" recommender falls outside Annex III and depends on the Annex I/MDR analysis. If a system does come in through Annex III, Article 6(3) allows it to escape high-risk classification only where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision-making, and where one of four conditions is met: (a) it performs a narrow procedural task; (b) it improves the result of a previously completed human activity; (c) it detects decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review; or (d) it performs a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to the Annex III use cases. Notwithstanding that, an Annex III system is always high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons. A tool that recommends a treatment to the treating clinician materially influences the outcome of decision-making and therefore would not normally qualify for that derogation. Separately, and independently of classification, if the software is intended to interact directly with natural persons, for example a patient-facing symptom or treatment assistant, Article 50(1) requires the provider to design it so those persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person in the circumstances and context of use; the law-enforcement carve-out in Article 50(1) is irrelevant here, and under Article 50(5) the information must be given clearly and distinguishably at the latest at the time of the first interaction and must meet applicable accessibility requirements.

Article 6(2)
Annex III (healthcare access/provision)

The answer states that the decisive route is Article 6(1), not Article 6(2), and argues that Annex III is a narrower fit, thereby contradicting the criterion that requires reliance on Article 6(2).

The answer explicitly states that treatment decision-support software does not fall under any listed use in Annex III, including point 5(a), and argues it falls outside Annex III, thus failing to affirm the required connection to Annex III (healthcare access/provision).

rows.question: About obligations of transparency to providers who want to use a GPAI model, do you need to disclose: date of release? number of paramaters? applicable model interaction with hardware? license? samples of outlier data used in training? Given clear yes/no to each item.
rows.answer: Yes to the date of release, yes to the number of parameters, yes to how the model interacts with hardware (where applicable), yes to the licence, and no to samples of outlier training data. The duty owed to providers who intend to integrate the model is Article 53(1)(b): the provider must draw up, keep up to date and make available information and documentation that enables those providers to understand the model's capabilities and limitations and to comply with their own obligations, containing at a minimum the elements of Annex XII, all without prejudice to intellectual property rights and confidential business information or trade secrets. Annex XII.1 requires a general description covering the tasks the model is intended to perform and the type and nature of AI systems into which it can be integrated; the applicable acceptable use policies; the date of release and methods of distribution; how the model interacts, or can be used to interact, with hardware or software that is not part of the model itself, where applicable; the versions of relevant software related to use of the model, where applicable; the architecture and number of parameters; the modality and format of inputs and outputs; and the licence for the model. Annex XII.2 adds the technical means required for integration, the modality and format of inputs and outputs and their maximum size, and information on the data used for training, testing and validation, where applicable, including the type and provenance of data and curation methodologies. Outlier data samples fall outside that list. Annex XII.2(c) calls only for descriptive information about the training, testing and validation data, type, provenance and curation methodology, not for disclosure of data instances, and the Act nowhere requires a downstream provider to be given samples of the corpus. The reference to outlier detection appears in Annex IV.2(d), which governs the technical documentation of high-risk AI systems, and even there it is a description of data-cleaning methodologies rather than sample data. Nor does Article 53(1)(d) change this: that is a publicly available summary of training content on the AI Office template, not sample disclosure. Two qualifications on the four affirmative items. First, the hardware-interaction element is expressly conditioned on "where applicable," so it is owed only where the model does or can interact with hardware or software outside itself. Second, under Article 53(2) the Article 53(1)(b) Annex XII obligation (together with the Article 53(1)(a) Annex XI obligation) does not apply to models released under a free and open-source licence allowing access, use, modification and distribution, with publicly available parameters including weights, architecture information and model usage information, unless the model is a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk under Article 51, in which case the full Article 53(1) duties apply regardless of licence.

Architecture and number of parameters - Yes
Interaction with hardware or software - Yes
License - Yes
Samples of outlier training data - No

The answer explicitly confirms disclosure of the number of parameters and references Annex XII.1, which includes 'the architecture and number of parameters' as required information.

The answer clearly states 'yes to the licence' and references Annex XII.1, which explicitly requires disclosure of the model licence.

The answer unambiguously states 'no to samples of outlier training data' and explains that Annex XII.2(c) requires only descriptive information, not data samples, and that no provision mandates disclosure of such samples.

rows.question: Name the areas of high-risk use cases. Is healthcare decision making one of them?
rows.answer: No, "healthcare decision-making" is not, as such, one of the listed high-risk areas; Annex III contains no general healthcare heading, and only certain health-related use-cases are caught. The eight areas listed in Annex III (Article 6(2)) are: biometrics (Annex III.1); critical infrastructure (Annex III.2); education and vocational training (Annex III.3); employment, workers' management and access to self-employment (Annex III.4); access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits (Annex III.5); law enforcement (Annex III.6); migration, asylum and border control management (Annex III.7); and administration of justice and democratic processes (Annex III.8). Only a lettered use-case under one of those headings makes a system high-risk on the Annex III route. Health-related systems become high-risk only where they match such a use-case, which under Annex III.5 covers AI used by or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate the eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, and to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim them (point (a)); risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in life and health insurance (point (c)); and evaluation and classification of emergency calls, dispatching or prioritising emergency first response services including medical aid, as well as emergency healthcare patient triage systems (point (d)). Clinical decision-support that falls outside those entries is instead captured, if at all, by the separate product route in Article 6(1): an AI system that is a safety component of, or is itself, a medical device or in vitro diagnostic device covered by Regulation (EU) 2017/745 or Regulation (EU) 2017/746 (Annex I, points 11 and 12) is high-risk where that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation. Even where an Annex III use-case is matched, Article 6(3) derogates: the system is not high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision-making, and it performs a narrow procedural task (point (a)), improves the result of a previously completed human activity (point (b)), detects decision-making patterns or deviations from prior patterns without being meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review (point (c)), or performs a preparatory task to a relevant assessment (point (d)); this derogation never applies where the system performs profiling of natural persons. The area list itself is not frozen: under Article 7(1) the Commission may by delegated act add or modify use-cases only where the system is intended to be used in an area already listed in Annex III and poses a risk equivalent to or greater than that of the systems already listed.
criteria_text: Biometrics; Critical infrastructure; Education and vocational training; Employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; Access to and enjoyment of essential private and public services and benefits; Law enforcement; Migration, asylum and border control management; Administration of justice and democratic processes
No

The answer clearly states that healthcare decision-making is not one of the listed high-risk areas as such, aligning with the 'No' in criterion 2.

rows.question: Could the introduction of guardrails in an AI agentic system reduce the risk of the system from high risk to moderate risk? What about changing the capabilities and intended use of the system?
rows.answer: No. Adding guardrails to an agentic system does not move it out of the high‑risk class, and the Act offers no "moderate risk" destination to move it to: outside the high‑risk regime what remains is the actor‑specific transparency duties of Article 50 (provider disclosure of AI interaction and machine‑readable marking of synthetic content; deployer disclosure for emotion recognition, biometric categorisation, deepfakes and public‑interest text) plus any voluntary measures. Classification under Article 6 is a function of route and purpose, not of residual risk after controls, Article 6(1) turns on the system being, or being a safety component of, an Annex I product that must undergo third‑party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation, and Article 6(2) turns on the system falling within a lettered use‑case under one of the eight Annex III areas. Neither limb asks how well the risk is mitigated. Guardrails are, on the contrary, the required output of high‑risk status: Article 9 obliges a documented, iterative risk‑management system that identifies foreseeable risks, estimates risks arising under reasonably foreseeable misuse, evaluates post‑market data and adopts targeted mitigation measures, and Article 8(1) requires compliance with Section 2 taking into account intended purpose and the state of the art, with Article 9 taken into account in doing so. Only the Commission can shrink the category, by delegated act under Article 7(3) read with Article 97, and only where the use‑case no longer poses any significant risk on the Article 7(2) criteria and deletion does not decrease the overall level of protection. The one qualification concerns guardrails that change what the system actually does rather than how safely it does it. Under the Article 6(3) derogation an Annex III system is not high‑risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision‑making, and it meets one of four conditions: it performs a narrow procedural task; it improves the result of a previously completed human activity; it detects decision‑making patterns or deviations from prior patterns without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment; or it performs a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to an Annex III use‑case. The derogation never applies where the system performs profiling of natural persons, which is high‑risk in all cases, and the provider must document its assessment before placing on the market or putting into service. Constraining an agent's tool access or outputs while it still performs the listed function does not satisfy any of those limbs. Yes as to the second lever: altering capabilities and intended use is the operative route, because intended purpose is what Article 6(2) tests against the Annex III use‑cases and Article 6(1) against the Annex I product scope. The change must be genuine and carried through the documentation chain, Article 13(3)(b) requires the instructions for use to state the intended purpose, the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance, and any circumstance under intended use or reasonably foreseeable misuse that may lead to Article 9(2) risks, and the deployer must use the system in accordance with those instructions under Article 26(1). The ratchet runs the other way as well: under Article 25(1)(b) and (c), a distributor, importer, deployer or third party that substantially modifies a high‑risk system so that it remains high‑risk, or modifies the intended purpose of a non‑high‑risk system so that it becomes high‑risk, itself becomes the provider with the full Article 16 obligations, the initial provider owing cooperation and technical access under Article 25(2). If the agent is built on a general‑purpose AI model, note separately that Article 51 systemic‑risk classification tracks high‑impact capabilities, with a presumption above 10^25 FLOPs of cumulative training compute, so deployment‑layer guardrails do not affect it.
criteria_text: No - guardrails alone do not create an intermediate "moderate risk" tier; the Act's Article 6(3) derogation is binary (high-risk or exempted)

Exemption applies only where the system's intended task itself meets one of four Article 6(3) conditions: narrow procedural task; improving a previously completed human activity; detecting deviations from prior decisions without replacing human assessment; or a preparatory task
Yes - changing the system's capabilities/intended use can exit high-risk status if the redefined task now satisfies one of those conditions
Exception: an AI system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk, regardless of guardrails or intended-use changes
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states that the Act does not create a 'moderate risk' tier and that the classification is binary under Article 6(3), thus satisfying the substance of the criterion.
The answer explicitly lists and explains the four conditions in Article 6(3) under which an Annex III system may not be considered high-risk, directly addressing the substance of the criterion.

The answer confirms that changing the system's capabilities and intended use can remove it from high-risk status if the new purpose meets one of the Article 6(3) conditions, which matches the criterion's substance.
The answer explicitly states that systems performing profiling of natural persons are always high-risk, regardless of guardrails or changes in use, thereby satisfying the exception criterion.

rows.question: Is the use of deep-fake images in university classes to represent e.g. skin conditions in patients allowed? Does the artificial nature of the content need to be disclosed for such an evidently educational and illustrative use? If so, does the lighter transparency requirement apply like for certain law enforcement situations?
rows.answer: Yes, the use is allowed, and yes, the artificial nature must be disclosed; no, the lighter "evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work" regime does not apply to clinical teaching images. Nothing in Article 5 prohibits generating synthetic dermatological imagery. The only education-specific prohibition, Article 5(1)(f), concerns inferring emotions of natural persons in educational institutions, which is not engaged by image generation; none of the other seven practices in Article 5(1), manipulative or deceptive techniques causing significant harm, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, individual criminal-risk profiling, untargeted facial-image scraping, biometric categorisation by sensitive attributes, or real-time remote biometric identification for law enforcement, is engaged either. Nor is the system automatically high-risk: under Article 6(2) a system is high-risk only if it falls within a use-case listed under one of the eight areas of Annex III, and producing illustrative teaching material is not one of the listed education and vocational-training use-cases. The transparency duty does bite. A photorealistic image of a skin condition on a person falls within the Article 3(60) definition of a deep fake, AI-generated image content resembling existing persons, objects, places, entities or events that would falsely appear to a person to be authentic. The university uses the system under its authority in a professional capacity and is therefore a deployer within Article 3(4), so the first subparagraph of Article 50(4) obliges it to disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. Under Article 50(5) that information must be given to the natural persons concerned, here the students, in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first exposure. Separately, and as a provider-side duty under Article 50(2), the generative system's outputs must be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated; the university inherits that duty only if it develops the system or puts it into service under its own name or trademark. The exceptions do not help. The image-deepfake duty in Article 50(4) is displaced only where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, that is a full exemption, not a lighter standard, and it is unavailable to a university. The reduced standard in the third subparagraph, disclosure of the existence of the generated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper display or enjoyment, is reserved for content forming part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work or programme; "analogous" must be read alongside those expressive categories, and didactic clinical illustration presented to students as a faithful depiction of real pathology is the opposite case, since its instructional value depends on students knowing whether they are looking at a real clinical photograph. Equally, the human-review and editorial-responsibility carve-out in the fourth subparagraph of Article 50(4) covers only AI-generated or manipulated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, so academic review of the teaching materials does not excuse the disclosure. Where the synthetic images are derived from or resemble identifiable real patients, data-protection law applies in parallel and independently of these obligations.
criteria_text: Yes, permitted
Disclosure still required under Article 50(4)
Lighter regime applies as "analogous work" to artistic/creative/fictional content — only existence of generated content must be disclosed, without hampering display/enjoyment
Law-enforcement carve-out is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and is inapplicable here
criterion_remarks: The answer states that the use is allowed, aligning with the substance that such use is not prohibited under Article 5 or otherwise.
The answer explicitly confirms the obligation to disclose under Article 50(4), stating the university must disclose the artificial nature of the content.
The answer rejects the applicability of the lighter regime for 'analogous work', arguing that educational clinical illustration does not fall under that category, contradicting the criterion.
The answer correctly identifies that the law-enforcement exception is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and confirms it does not apply in this context.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose with logical flow, suitable for regulatory guidance.

rows.question: A supermarket uses an AI tool that analyzes only current-cart and checkout anomalies (no biometrics, no face recognition, no sensitive-trait inference, no cross-context social scoring) to flag transactions for optional manual bag checks by store staff. The retailer claims this is "high risk like policing", as it: resembles investigation of potentially criminal offences (theft) + evaluates or classifies persons based on observed behaviour in a way that may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment. Is this situation potentially high-risk?
rows.answer: No. On the facts given, this is neither a prohibited practice nor a high-risk AI system, so the retailer's "high risk like policing" characterisation is not sustained. The social-scoring prohibition is not engaged. Article 5(1), point (c) catches only the evaluation or classification of natural persons over a certain period of time on the basis of their social behaviour or known, inferred or predicted personal or personality characteristics, where the resulting social score leads to either or both of: (i) detrimental or unfavourable treatment in social contexts unrelated to the context in which the data was originally generated or collected; or (ii) detrimental or unfavourable treatment that is unjustified or disproportionate to the social behaviour or its gravity. A tool scoring only the current cart and checkout event produces no cross-temporal social score; the consequence, an optional bag check by store staff at the same till, occurs in the very context in which the data arose, and is a proportionate response to a checkout anomaly. Both limbs of point (c) therefore fail. The criminal-offence limb is likewise not engaged. Article 5(1), point (d) prohibits AI systems making risk assessments to assess or predict the risk of a natural person committing a criminal offence, where based solely on profiling or on assessing personality traits and characteristics; and it expressly does not apply to systems supporting the human assessment of a person's involvement in criminal activity that is already based on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to that activity. Here the flag rests on observed transaction facts, not profiling or personality traits, and it merely supports a staff decision, squarely within that carve-out. Points (a), (b), (f) and (g) are not in issue absent manipulation, vulnerability exploitation, biometrics or emotion inference. Nor does Annex III apply: its law-enforcement area (Annex III, point 6) covers use by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, not a private retailer's own loss-prevention tool, and no other listed use-case fits. Article 5(8) leaves other Union law, notably data protection, unaffected.
criteria_text: No
Annex III.6 categories apply only where the AI system is used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or by Union institutions/bodies in support of law enforcement authorities)

A supermarket's own loss-prevention/bag-check tool, run by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, so it falls outside Annex III.6 regardless of its resemblance to investigative or evaluative functions
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No' as its unambiguous position, matching the required verdict.
The answer explicitly states that Annex III.6 applies only to use by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, and that the supermarket's tool does not meet this condition.
The answer directly explains that a private retailer's loss-prevention tool, used by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, and therefore falls outside Annex III.6.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear legal prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents a coherent, actionable analysis.

rows.question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
rows.answer: No. Applying harmonised standards to avoid the third‑party route does not release you from Chapter III, Section 2; it is precisely the condition on which that opt‑out is made available. For a high-risk AI system covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, Article 43(3) provides that the provider follows the relevant sectoral conformity assessment procedure and that "[t]he requirements set out in Section 2 of this Chapter shall apply to those high-risk AI systems and shall be part of that assessment." The same paragraph then addresses the operator's exact situation: where a Section A act enables the product manufacturer to opt out of a third-party conformity assessment on condition that it has applied all harmonised standards covering all the relevant requirements, "that manufacturer may use that option only if it has also applied harmonised standards or, where applicable, common specifications referred to in Article 41, covering all requirements set out in Section 2 of this Chapter." The opt-out is therefore not an exemption from Section 2 but a substitute route to demonstrating it: if you did not also apply harmonised standards or Article 41 common specifications covering every Section 2 requirement, risk management (Article 9), data and data governance (Article 10), technical documentation (Article 11 and Annex IV), record-keeping (Article 12), transparency and provision of information to deployers (Article 13), human oversight (Article 14), and accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity (Article 15), you were not entitled to use the opt-out at all, and the product's conformity assessment is defective. The classification is unaffected. Article 6(1) makes the system high-risk where it is intended to be used as a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by Annex I legislation and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment for placing on the market or putting into service; the conditional opt-out in a Section A act is the legislature's own premise in Article 43(3), which presupposes such systems remain within scope and regulates the opt-out rather than removing the AI system from Section 2. Note also that Annex VI internal control is the Annex III route under Article 43(1) and is not what the operator's product follows, the operator's obligations run through the sectoral procedure, to which points 4.3, 4.4, 4.5 and the fifth paragraph of point 4.6 of Annex VII also apply. Two further consequences follow. Where the sectoral act's notified body is nonetheless involved, it may control conformity with Section 2 only if its compliance with Article 31(4), (5), (10) and (11) was assessed in the notification procedure under that act. And under Article 43(4), a substantial modification triggers a new conformity assessment, regardless of whether the modified system is further distributed or continues to be used by the current deployer; changes pre-determined by you at the initial assessment and documented under point 2(f) of Annex IV for a system that continues to learn do not count as substantial modification.
criteria_text: No
Section 2 requirements still apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment (Art. 43(3), second sentence)
The third-party opt-out under sectoral legislation is available only if harmonised standards/common specifications applied cover ALL Section 2 requirements, not just the sectoral ones
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states 'No' as its opening and unambiguous position, satisfying the bare verdict requirement.
The answer cites Article 43(3), second sentence, and explains that Section 2 requirements apply and are part of the sectoral conformity assessment, stating the substance required.

The answer clearly states that the opt-out is conditional on applying harmonised standards or common specifications covering *all* Section 2 requirements, not just the sectoral ones, which captures the full substance of the criterion.
